intro.heading: You have run the training. Now you need to know it landed.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care homes.
intro.paragraph: A trainer has spent a morning on safeguarding training with the day team. The room was full, the feedback forms were warm and everyone signed the attendance sheet. Two weeks later the manager realises they cannot say what each person took away. Some carers joined from overseas and say little in group sessions. Others came straight off a night shift. The manager has a signature for each of them and nothing more, and an inspector will not accept a signature as an answer. Here is how that plays out.

trail.text: A trainer runs safeguarding for the day team.
The room is full. The feedback forms are warm.
The manager is on the floor and cannot say what everyone took away.
Two carers who joined from overseas last year and say little in group sessions.
A carer who came off a night shift and was fighting to stay awake.
Three signatures. Nothing that shows what the three understood.
“What would you do if you suspected abuse?” A signature is not an answer.

trail_close: The session was never the problem. The gap is between the session and the evidence. Here is how CareStream fills it, using your own policies, without replacing the session.

why.heading: A signature shows who was in the room, not what they understood
why.sub: An inspector will not ask who attended. They will ask a carer what they would do.

cards.title: Quiet nods are not understanding
cards.body: Some carers follow every word. Others nod because the session moved fast, they were tired after a night shift, or English is their second language.

cards.title: Memory fades within weeks
cards.body: Nobody checks what people remember two weeks later, so a gap can sit unseen until an incident or an inspection brings it out.

cards.title: Chasing it by hand does not scale
cards.body: Writing extra training for every missed point, for every carer, is work no manager has time for. Without it, the gap simply stays open.

talk.heading: The questions managers ask, and how CareStream answers them
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. The questions are the ones we hear most.

items.q: We have just paid for a trainer. Why would I add anything on top?
items.a: You would not be replacing the trainer. You would be adding a check after the session, so that you know what people took in. The session teaches. The follow up shows whether it worked. That is blended learning: the room teaches, and CareStream checks and closes the gaps.

items.q: How would I know whether my carers understood it?
items.a: After the session you allocate short training on that topic, built from your own policies. Each carer completes it in the Staff Hub on their own phone, and their answers are scored, so you can see who understood and who did not.

items.q: What happens when someone gets a question wrong?
items.a: It goes straight into that carer's Follow-up tab in the hub, and they get an email. They choose Learn & retry, a short lesson on that exact point (why it matters, what to remember and a realistic situation) followed by a fresh question, or Just retry the same question. They can retry as often as they need. You do not have to write or chase anything.

items.q: Is that lesson generic, or about how we work?
items.a: It is built from your own policies. The lesson draws on the text your service has written, so it teaches what you actually do and not what a textbook says. Where your policies do not cover a point, it falls back on general good practice, which is a prompt to improve the policy.

items.q: Some of my carers speak English as a second language. Does that matter?
items.a: It matters a great deal. A carer who answers wrongly may understand the topic perfectly and still miss a word. They can open the lesson in their own language, so a wrong answer points to a gap in knowledge and not in vocabulary. Translation is part of the paid plans, and the reminder emails are in English.

items.q: What do I see across the team?
items.a: The Knowledge gaps view in the training reporting shows the questions most often missed, the weakest topics and how gaps are being closed, and a digest arrives on Monday. That tells you whether one person needs a conversation or the session itself needs a tweak.

items.q: Does this replace practical sign off, like watching someone use a hoist?
items.a: No. A competent person still needs to show and observe hands on skills. CareStream checks understanding and keeps the record. It does not replace the observation.

items.q: What could I show an inspector?
items.a: A record of what each person was asked, what they got wrong, the lesson they were given and whether it then landed. That goes further than a signature, because it shows staff are competent as well as trained. It sits alongside the rest of your CQC evidence.

faqs.heading: Face to face training and CareStream, answered

items.q: Does online training replace face to face training?
items.a: No. For topics such as moving and handling, a competent person must still show and observe the technique. CareStream sits alongside the session and shows what people retained.

items.q: Where does the follow up training come from?
items.a: From your own policies. You pick the topic module, and CareStream builds the lessons and questions from the policy text, so it matches what your service does. You can edit and preview it before you assign it.

items.q: What if a carer gets a question wrong?
items.a: It appears in their Follow-up tab. They can choose Learn & retry, a short lesson on that point followed by a fresh question, or Just retry the same question, as often as they need. Treat it as information, not failure.

items.q: How soon after the session should the follow up go out?
items.a: Within a few days is a sensible rule: early enough that the session is fresh, late enough to show what stuck. You choose when to allocate it, and you can set a due date.

items.q: Face to face vs online training: which is better?
items.a: Neither replaces the other. A room is good for discussion and hands on demonstration, and a competent person must still show and observe practical skills. Online follow up is good for checking understanding and closing gaps. Used together, this is blended learning.

items.q: Is face to face safeguarding training enough on its own?
items.a: A good session is a strong start, but safeguarding training only protects people if staff remember it when it matters. A short follow up built from your own safeguarding policy shows who understood and who needs another look. The safeguarding course covers the topic itself.

items.q: How to measure training effectiveness in a care home
items.a: Look at four things: whether people liked the training, whether they learned it, whether they act differently on the floor, and whether outcomes improve. A knowledge check after the session covers learning, observation covers behaviour and audits show results. CareStream covers the knowledge check and the follow up.

items.q: Will an inspector accept this as evidence?
items.a: The Care Quality Commission looks for staff who are competent in their role, not only trained. A record of questions, lessons and results helps show that. See Regulation 18 on staffing for the wording.

items.q: What are the CQC training requirements for care home staff?
items.a: Regulation 18 says staff must receive the support, training, professional development, supervision and appraisal they need to carry out their duties. It does not list courses, so each provider decides what its staff need and must be able to show it. The CQC guidance on Regulation 18 explains how inspectors look at it.

guide.heading: A practical way to follow up face to face training
guide.lede: Care home staff training does not end when the session does. A session ends, a sheet is signed and everyone returns to the floor. The follow up is where a manager learns whether the day worked.

sections.h3: Training evaluation that fits a busy service
paragraphs: Evaluating training effectiveness does not need to be complicated. The Kirkpatrick model, a widely used way of measuring training effectiveness, separates four things: whether people liked the session, whether they learned from it, whether they now act differently on the floor, and whether outcomes improve. Feedback forms cover the first. A knowledge check after the session covers the second. Observation and audits cover the rest.

sections.h3: Four checks that fit a busy service
checklist: Within a week: allocate short training on the topic of the session, built from your policies.
Whenever an answer is wrong: the carer opens a short lesson on that point, then a fresh question.
Each month: look at the most missed questions and the weakest topics.
On the floor: one observed example for skills that need hands on practice. This remains your staff competency assessment for hands on skills.

guide.note: For the inspector. Keep the questions, the lessons and the results together, so you can show understanding as well as attendance.
